 1            Plaintiffs Cassandra Edwards, Everett Scott, Allan Amsel, and Brittany Frank (“Plaintiffs”)

 2   and Defendants Apple Inc. and AppleCare Service Company, Inc. (“Apple”) hereby agree that the

 3   following procedures shall govern discovery of Electronically-Stored Information (“ESI”) in this

 4   case:

 5            1.     Search. The parties agree that in responding to an initial Fed. R. Civ. P. 34 request, or

 6   earlier if appropriate, they will meet and confer about methods to search ESI in order to identify ESI

 7   that is subject to production in discovery and filter out ESI that is not subject to discovery.

 8   Notwithstanding prior agreement on the search terms to be used for electronic searches, should a

 9   search produce an unreasonably large number of non-responsive or irrelevant results, the parties shall

10   (at the producing party’s request) meet and confer to discuss application of further negative search

11   restrictions (e.g., if a single search was for “card” and ninety percent of the resulting documents came

12   from the irrelevant term “credit card,” a negative limitation to ignore documents only returned as a

13   result of “credit card” may be applied to remove these documents). The party receiving production

14   shall not unreasonably oppose such further restrictions designed to filter immaterial search results.

15   The parties shall make good faith efforts to identify appropriate email custodians and produce email

16   on the agreed upon schedule, but reserve the right to seek email from additional email custodians

17   identified through discovery.

18            2.     Cooperation. The parties are aware of the importance the Court places on

19   cooperation and commit to cooperate in good faith throughout the matter consistent with this Court’s

20   Guidelines for the Discovery of ESI.

21            3.     Format for production of documents – documents existing in electronic format.

22   Except as otherwise provided for in this Stipulation, all documents existing in electronic format shall

23   be produced in multiple page, searchable PDF format at a resolution of at least 300 dpi in accordance

24   with the following:

25                   A.     PDF files shall be produced along with Concordance/Opticon image load files

26   that indicate the beginning and ending of each document.

27

                                   9          E.      Conversion (Count V)

                                  10          Conversion is the wrongful exercise of dominion over the property of another.” Mindys

                                  11   Cosmetics, Inc. v. Dakar, 611 F.3d 590, 601 (9th Cir. 2010) (internal quotation marks omitted).

                                  12   The elements of a conversion claim are: (1) the plaintiff’s ownership or right to possession of the
Northern District of California
 United States District Court




                                  13   property at the time of the conversion; (2) the defendant’s conversion by a wrongful act or

                                  14   disposition of property rights; and (3) damages. Id. The alleged converter must have assumed

                                  15   control over the property or applied the property to his own use. Id. A conversion claim for

                                  16   money is not stated “unless there is a specific, identifiable sum involved, such as where an agent

                                  17   accepts a sum of money to be paid to another and fails to make the payment.” Kim v. Westmoore

                                  18   Partners, Inc., 201 Cal.App.4th 267, 284 (2011) (citing McKell v. Wash. Mut., Inc., 142

                                  19   Cal.App.4th 1457, 1491 (2006)).

                                  20          That said, “[n]ot every failure to deliver property to the rightful owner constitutes a

                                  21   conversion . . . To establish a conversion, it is incumbent upon the plaintiff to show an intention or

                                  22   purpose to convert the goods and to exercise ownership over them, or to prevent the owner from

                                  23   taking possession of the property.” Spates v. Dameron Hosp. Ass’n, 114 Cal.App.4th 208, 222

                                  24   (2003) (internal citation and quotation marks omitted). In other words, “conversion can occur

                                  25   when a willful failure to return property deprives the owner of possession.” Fearon v. Dep’t of

                                  26   Corr., 162 Cal.App.3d 1254, 1257 (1984) (emphasis added) (citing Schroeder v. Auto Driveaway

                                  27   Co., 11 Cal. 3d 908, 918 (1974)).

                                   1          Whether certain types of over- or unlawful charges can constitute conversion is an open

                                   2   question in California. See Welco Electronics, Inc. v. Mora, 223 Cal.App.4th 202, 211 (2014)

                                   3   (finding defendant’s unauthorized charges to plaintiff’s credit card deprived plaintiff of “property

                                   4   rights – i.e., money from the available credit line belonging to plaintiff with the credit card

                                   5   company”); Worldwide Travel, Inc. v. Travelmate US, Inc., No. 14-CV-00155-BAS DHB, 2015

                                   6   WL 1013704, at *10 (S.D. Cal. Mar. 9, 2015) (finding no conversion where parties’ dispute was

                                   7   about the amount and appropriateness of the charges, but plaintiffs had otherwise “authorized

                                   8   Defendants to make monthly charges as payment for Defendants’ advertising services”).

                                   9          After reviewing the body of authority on conversion in this district, the Court finds that, on

                                  10   these specific facts, Plaintiffs have successfully alleged a conversion claim. For Amsel and

                                  11   Edwards, at least, the terms of the Plan were crystal clear: by trading-in their devices to an Apple

                                  12   store, they sufficiently “express[ed]” their intent to cancel their Plans. Under the Plan, once these
Northern District of California
 United States District Court




                                  13   terms are met, the Plan “will be cancelled.” Plan § 9.3. When Amsel and Edwards traded-in their

                                  14   iPhones, Apple (or Apple’s vendor) gained actual possession of the devices and all associated

                                  15   property interests. AC ¶¶ 50-52. To continue charging Plaintiffs in such circumstances is

                                  16   essentially theft because Plaintiffs lose money and in return receive no possible benefit. Id. ¶ 53

                                  17   (“Because AppleCare+ is an extended warranty and service plan for a specific device, it becomes

                                  18   worthless once a consumer no longer owns the Covered Device.”).

                                  19          The Court is not persuaded that Plaintiffs’ initial consent to be charged for AppleCare+ at

                                  20   purchase somehow permits later credit card charges after consent had been rescinded. Plaintiffs

                                  21   consented to automatic renewal only “unless and until cancelled.” Plan § 9.3. Apple promised

                                  22   that the AppleCare+ plan “will be cancelled” upon trade-in. Id. Consequently, the distinction

                                  23   between whether the trade-in itself constitutes cancellation of the Plan or is merely the

                                  24   manifestation of Plaintiffs’ intent to have Apple cancel the Plans is a distinction without a

                                  25   difference. The salient point is that Amsel and Edwards, at least, withdrew their authorization for

                                  26   automatic, monthly charges when they tendered their iPhones to Apple; the very terms of the Plan

                                  27   say as much. At that point, the devices were legally owned by Apple (or Apple’s vendor), and

                                  28   they had actual knowledge it was within their possession. AC ¶ 52. Nevertheless, Apple
                                                                                         16

                                   1   continued to charge Amsel and Edwards for a service on a device they no longer owned. Id.

                                   3   possession, would consent to continuing to make payment for AppleCare+ on a device that was no

                                   4   longer theirs.

                                   6          F.        Civil Theft, Cal. Penal Code § 496 (Count VI)

                                   7          “Section 496(a) defines the criminal offense of what is commonly referred to as receiving

                                   8   stolen property, while section 496(c) sets forth a right to special civil remedies where a violation

                                   9   of section 496(a) has occurred.” Switzer v. Wood, 35 Cal. App. 5th 116, 125-26 (2019), as

                                  10   modified (May 10, 2019). “While section 496(a) covers a spectrum of impermissible activity

                                  11   relating to stolen property, the elements required to show a violation of section 496(a) are simply

                                  12   that (i) property was stolen or obtained in a manner constituting theft, (ii) the defendant knew the

                                  13   property was so stolen or obtained, and (iii) the defendant received or had possession of the stolen

                                  16   the statute. Siry Inv., L.P. v. Farkhondehpour, 13 Cal. 5th 333, 361 (2022). It observed that

                                  17                    not all commercial or consumer disputes alleging that a defendant
                                                        obtained money or property through fraud, misrepresentation, or
                                  18                    breach of a contractual promise will amount to a theft. To prove theft,
                                                        a plaintiff must establish criminal intent on the part of the defendant
                                  19                    beyond “mere proof of nonperformance or actual falsity.” This
                                                        requirement prevents “ ‘[o]rdinary commercial defaults’ ” from being
                                  20                    transformed into a theft. If misrepresentations or unfulfilled promises
                                                        “are made innocently or inadvertently, they can no more form the

                                                        can an innocent breach of contract.”

                                       Id. at 361-62 (quoting People v. Ashley, 42 Cal.2d 246, 264 (1954)). In other words, a defendant
                                  23
                                       must have “acted not innocently or inadvertently, but with careful planning and deliberation
                                  24
                                       reflecting the requisite criminal intent.” Id.

                                  26

                                       inadvertently . . . can no more form the basis for a prosecution for obtaining property by false
                                  28

                                   1   pretenses than can an innocent breach of contract.” Id. (quoting Ashley, 42 Cal. 2d at 264).

                                   3   time knowledge that it was charging putative class members for AppleCare+ on devices that

                                   4   Plaintiffs no longer owned and had returned to Apple. AC ¶ 52. Rather than cancelling

                                   5   AppleCare+ as promised upon trade-in, Apple continued to charge Plaintiffs and putative class

                                   6   members for the service, sometimes for years. See AC ¶¶ 14-17; id. ¶ 56 (excerpting dozens of

                                   7   internet comments from 2020 through 2024 in which individuals alleged that Apple continued to

                                   8   charge them for AppleCare+ after trade-in). Amsel himself alleges that Apple refused to provide a
